usamo-usajmo-2025-01.title: Consecutive differences are bad values
usamo-usajmo-2025-01.body:
Suppose, for contradiction, that the set $S$ of integers $c$ for which $g_c(x) = f(x) + cx$ is not a bijection is finite.

**Every consecutive difference lies in $S$.** For any integer $x$, let $c = f(x) - f(x+1)$. Then
$$g_c(x+1) - g_c(x) = f(x+1) - f(x) + c = 0,$$
so $g_c$ is not injective and $c \in S$. Thus $S$ is nonempty, and with $M = \max_{s \in S}|s|$ we get $|f(x+1) - f(x)| \le M$ for all integers $x$.

**A large $c$ fails.** Let $c = M + 2$; then $c \notin S$, so $g_c$ should be a bijection. But for every $x$,
$$g_c(x+1) - g_c(x) = f(x+1) - f(x) + M + 2 \ge -M + M + 2 = 2.$$
So $g_c$ is strictly increasing with steps of at least $2$: $g_c(x) \ge g_c(0) + 2$ for $x \ge 1$ and $g_c(x) \le g_c(0) - 2$ for $x \le -1$. The integer $g_c(0) + 1$ is never attained, so $g_c$ is not surjective — a contradiction.

Hence infinitely many $c$ make $g$ fail to be a bijection. ∎

usamo-usajmo-2025-02.title: The last $\ell$ digits are an odd multiple of $n^\ell$
usamo-usajmo-2025-02.body:
Let $b = 2n$ with $n$ odd, and let $\ell$ be an integer with $1 \le \ell \le k$.

**Claim.** The remainder $r_\ell$ of $n^k$ upon division by $b^\ell = 2^\ell n^\ell$ equals $c\,n^\ell$ for some odd integer $c$ with $1 \le c \le 2^\ell - 1$.

*Proof.* Since $n^\ell$ divides both $n^k$ and $b^\ell$, it divides $r_\ell = n^k - qb^\ell$; write $r_\ell = c\,n^\ell$ with $0 \le c < 2^\ell$. Also $2^\ell \mid b^\ell$, so $r_\ell \equiv n^k \pmod{2^\ell}$, which is odd. Hence $c\,n^\ell$ is odd, so $c$ is odd and $c \ge 1$. $\square$

**Finish.** Suppose $n \ge (d+1)2^{k-1}$. Then $(2n)^{k-1} = 2^{k-1}n^{k-1} \le n^k < (2n)^k$, so $n^k$ has exactly $k$ digits in base $2n$. The $\ell$-th digit from the right is $\left\lfloor r_\ell / b^{\ell-1}\right\rfloor$, and by the claim
$$\frac{r_\ell}{b^{\ell-1}} \ge \frac{n^\ell}{2^{\ell-1}n^{\ell-1}} = \frac{n}{2^{\ell-1}} \ge \frac{n}{2^{k-1}} \ge d + 1.$$
So each of the $k$ digits is at least $d + 1 > d$. This holds for every odd $n \ge (d+1)2^{k-1}$. ∎

usamo-usajmo-2025-03.title: Tileable iff balanced, then a shifting bijection
usamo-usajmo-2025-03.body:
Let $R$ have $2n$ columns and $2m$ rows. An up-right path is determined by the heights $0 \le h_1 \le h_2 \le \dots \le h_{2n} \le 2m$, where the region *below* the path consists of the bottom $h_i$ cells of column $i$; the region above consists of the top $2m - h_i$ cells of column $i$. Color the cells like a chessboard, the cell in column $i$ and row $r$ (from the bottom) being black when $i + r$ is even.

Call a region a *staircase* if it consists of the bottom $h_i$ cells of column $i$ for a nondecreasing sequence $(h_i)$. The region above the path, rotated by $180^\circ$, is also a staircase, and this rotation preserves the chessboard coloring of the $2m \times 2n$ board up to swapping colors.

**Lemma.** A staircase can be tiled by dominoes if and only if it has as many black cells as white cells.

*Proof.* A domino covers one cell of each color, so the condition is necessary. For sufficiency, induct on the number of cells; the empty staircase is fine. Let a nonempty balanced staircase have nonzero heights $h_1 \le \dots \le h_N$ (drop empty columns), and let $L_r = \#\{i : h_i \ge r\}$ be the length of row $r$; rows are right-aligned and $L_1 \ge L_2 \ge \cdots$. Two kinds of moves remove dominoes and leave a staircase:
1. If $h_i \ge h_{i-1} + 2$ for some $i$ (with $h_0 := 0$), remove the top two cells of each of the columns $i, i+1, \dots, N$ (vertical dominoes). The new heights $h_j - 2$ ($j \ge i$) are still $\ge h_{i-1}$, so the result is a staircase.
2. If two columns have the same height $r$, i.e. $L_r \ge L_{r+1} + 2$, remove the leftmost two cells of each of the rows $1, 2, \dots, r$ (horizontal dominoes; each of these rows has length $\ge L_r \ge 2$). The new lengths $L_j - 2$ ($j \le r$) are still $\ge L_{r+1}$, so the result is a staircase.

The removed cells are balanced, so the rest is balanced and can be tiled by induction. If neither move applies, then $h_1 = 1$, consecutive heights differ by at most $1$, and all heights are distinct; so the heights are exactly $1, 2, \dots, N$. In that staircase column $i$ has $i$ cells, which are balanced for even $i$ and have one extra black cell for odd $i$ (its bottom cell $(i, 1)$ is black). So it has $\lceil N/2\rceil > 0$ more black than white cells — not balanced. Hence a move always applies. $\square$

**Counting.** The whole board has $2mn$ cells of each color, so the region above the path is balanced exactly when the region below is. By the lemma we must count sequences $(h_i)$ whose lower region is balanced. Column $i$'s lower part (rows $1, \dots, h_i$) is balanced if $h_i$ is even; if $h_i$ is odd it has one extra black cell when $i$ is odd and one extra white cell when $i$ is even. So, with
$$a = \#\{i \text{ even}: h_i \text{ odd}\}, \qquad b = \#\{i \text{ odd} : h_i \text{ odd}\},$$
the path works if and only if $a = b$.

Now set $t_i = h_i + i$. The map $(h_i) \mapsto \{t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_{2n}\}$ is a bijection from nondecreasing sequences with values in $[0, 2m]$ to $2n$-element subsets of $\{1, 2, \dots, 2m + 2n\}$. The number $t_i$ is odd exactly when ($i$ even and $h_i$ odd) or ($i$ odd and $h_i$ even). There are $n$ odd indices $i$, so
$$\#\{i : t_i \text{ odd}\} = a + (n - b), \qquad \#\{i : t_i \text{ even}\} = 2n - a - n + b = n - a + b.$$
These are equal if and only if $a = b$. So we must count the $2n$-subsets of $\{1, \dots, 2m + 2n\}$ with exactly $n$ odd and $n$ even elements. That set has $m + n$ odd and $m + n$ even numbers, so the count is
$$\binom{m+n}{n}\binom{m+n}{n} = \binom{m+n}{m}^2.$$

**Answer:** $\dbinom{m+n}{m}^2$. ∎

usamo-usajmo-2025-04.title: Induction on the number of terms
usamo-usajmo-2025-04.body:
We prove the statement for all $n \ge 0$ by induction (for $n = 0$ the left side is $0$ and the right side is $\ge 0$).

Let $n \ge 1$ and put $s = a_0 + a_1 + \dots + a_{n-1}$. The induction hypothesis (for the sequence $a_0 \ge \dots \ge a_{n-1}$) gives
$$\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} i\binom{a_i}{2} \le \frac12\binom{s}{2},$$
so it suffices to prove
$$n\binom{a_n}{2} \le \frac12\left[\binom{s + a_n}{2} - \binom{s}{2}\right].$$
Since $\binom{s + a}{2} - \binom s2 = sa + \binom a2$, this is
$$n\,a_n(a_n - 1) \le a_n s + \frac{a_n(a_n - 1)}{2}.$$
Each of $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ is at least $a_n$, so $s \ge n a_n$, and $a_n \ge 0$. Therefore
$$a_n s + \frac{a_n(a_n-1)}2 \ge n a_n^2 + \frac{a_n(a_n - 1)}{2} \ge n a_n^2 \ge n a_n(a_n - 1),$$
where the middle step uses $a_n(a_n - 1) \ge 0$ for integers $a_n \ge 0$. This completes the induction. ∎

*Remark.* The bound is far from tight; equality holds only when $a_0 \in \{0, 1\}$ and all other $a_i = 0$.

usamo-usajmo-2025-05.title: The center lies on the perpendicular to $BC$ at $C$
usamo-usajmo-2025-05.body:
Let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$ with center $O$, and let $Q$ be the point of $\Gamma$ diametrically opposite $B$. Since the triangle is acute, $Q \ne A, C$, and by Thales $QA \perp AB$ and $QC \perp BC$.

**Fact.** $P$ lies on $\Gamma$ and on line $AH$. (Standard: $P$ is on the altitude $AH \perp BC$, and the reflection of $H$ in $BC$ lies on the circumcircle because $\angle BPC = \angle BHC = 180^\circ - \angle A$.)

Let $M$ be the midpoint of $QC$. We show $M$ is the circumcenter of $AFP$.

**$MA = MP$.** Lines $AP$ (the altitude from $A$) and $QC$ are both perpendicular to $BC$, hence parallel. The perpendicular bisectors of the chords $AP$ and $QC$ of $\Gamma$ both pass through $O$ and are both perpendicular to this common direction, so they are the same line. It contains $M$, so $MA = MP$.

**$MA = MF$.** Lines $QA$ and $CF$ are both perpendicular to $AB$, so $AQCF$ is a trapezoid with parallel sides $AQ$ and $FC$ and legs $AF$ and $QC$. The segment joining the midpoints of the legs is parallel to the parallel sides; so if $N$ is the midpoint of $AF$, then $MN \parallel AQ \perp AB$. Thus $M$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AF$ (a segment on line $AB$), and $MA = MF$.

So $M$ is the center of the circle $(AFP)$. The chord $XY$ of this circle lies on $BC$, and the foot of the perpendicular from the center $M$ to $BC$ is the midpoint of $XY$. But $M$ lies on line $QC \perp BC$, so this foot is $C$. Hence $C$ is the midpoint of $XY$, i.e. $CX = CY$. ∎

usamo-usajmo-2025-06.title: Strong induction with three prime cases
usamo-usajmo-2025-06.body:
We show by induction on $N \ge 2025$ that $\{1, \dots, N\} \subseteq S$; the base case is given. Assume $\{1, \dots, N\} \subseteq S$.

Call a positive integer *good* if every prime power $q^f$ exactly dividing it satisfies $q^f \le N$. **Good numbers are in $S$:** their prime-power factors are pairwise coprime elements of $S$, and multiplying them in one at a time uses the second property repeatedly.

If $N + 1$ is composite, then $N \in S$ and $N + 1$ is composite, so all divisors of $N + 1$, including $N + 1$, are in $S$. So assume $N + 1 = p$ is a prime, $p \ge 2027$. It suffices to find $s \in S$ with $s + 1 \in \{p^2, 2p\}$ (both composite, both divisible by $p$). Since $p$ is odd, $p - 1$ and $p + 1$ are even, and they cannot both be powers of $2$ (powers of $2$ differing by $2$ are $2, 4$).

**Case 1: neither $p - 1$ nor $p + 1$ is a power of $2$.** Take $s = p^2 - 1 = (p-1)(p+1)$; we show it is good. Since $\gcd(p-1, p+1) = 2$, an odd prime power exactly dividing $s$ divides one of $p \pm 1$, which is even, so it is at most $\frac{p+1}2 < p$. For the power of $2$: one of $p \pm 1$ is $\equiv 2 \pmod 4$, and the other, $u$, is not a power of $2$, so the power of $2$ in $u$ is at most $u/3$; hence the power of $2$ exactly dividing $s$ is at most $2u/3 \le \frac{2(p+1)}3 < p$. So $s$ is good, $s \in S$, and $s + 1 = p^2$.

**Case 2: $p + 1 = 2^q$.** Then $q \ge 11$, and $q$ is odd (if $q$ were even, $3 \mid 2^q - 1 = p$). First,
$$2^{q+1} - 1 = \left(2^{(q+1)/2} - 1\right)\left(2^{(q+1)/2} + 1\right),$$
a product of two coprime odd numbers (they differ by $2$), both less than $p = 2^q - 1$, hence both in $S$. So $2^{q+1} - 1 \in S$, and since $2^{q+1}$ is composite, $2^{q+1} \in S$. Now
$$p^2 - 1 = (p-1)(p+1) = 2(2^{q-1} - 1)\cdot 2^q = 2^{q+1}\left(2^{q-1} - 1\right).$$
The odd number $2^{q-1} - 1 < p$ is in $S$ and is coprime to $2^{q+1} \in S$, so $s = p^2 - 1 \in S$ with $s + 1 = p^2$.

**Case 3: $p - 1 = 2^t$.** Then $t \ge 11$, and $t$ is even (if $t$ were odd, $3 \mid 2^t + 1 = p$). So $p = 2^t + 1 \equiv 1 + 1 = 2 \pmod 3$, and $s = 2p - 1 = 2^{t+1} + 1$ is divisible by $3$.

*$s$ is not a power of $3$.* If $2^a + 1 = 3^j$ with $a \ge 1$: for $j$ odd, $3^j - 1 \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ forces $a = 1$; for $j = 2i$ even, $(3^i - 1)(3^i + 1) = 2^a$ is a product of two powers of $2$ differing by $2$, so they are $2, 4$ and $a = 3$. Here $a = t + 1 \ge 12$, so this is impossible.

*$s$ is good.* Let $3^e$ exactly divide $s$; the cofactor $s/3^e > 1$ is odd and coprime to $3$, so it is at least $5$, giving $3^e \le s/5 < p$. Any other prime power exactly dividing $s$ divides $s/3$, so it is at most $\frac{2p-1}{3} < p$. So $s \in S$ and $s + 1 = 2p$.

In every case $p = N + 1 \in S$, completing the induction. Hence $S$ contains every positive integer. ∎
